blocks.prompt: The Brush and the Tiny Bugs
blocks.text: A toothbrush has two parts. The handle is for your hand. The bristles are for your teeth. The bristles are made of nylon, which is a kind of plastic. Long ago, brushes had stiff hair from a pig. The hair got soggy and it never dried. Nylon dries fast, so we use it now. Your mouth is full of tiny living things called bacteria. They eat the sugar left on your teeth. Then they make acid, and the acid makes holes. The brush wipes them off before they can. Brush for two minutes. That is longer than you think. Sing a song while you brush.

blocks.prompt: Why the Bristles Are Soft
blocks.text: For most of history, a toothbrush was a stick. People in Babylon frayed the end of a twig and rubbed it on their teeth. That was more than five thousand years ago. In many parts of the world, people still clean their teeth with a chewing stick called a miswak, and it works well. The brush you know was invented in China. Makers pulled stiff bristles from the neck of a hog and set them into a handle carved from bone or bamboo. In 1780, an Englishman named William Addis was sitting in prison. He saved a bone from his dinner, drilled small holes in it, and pushed in bristles he got from a guard. When he was let out, he began making brushes to sell. The company he started still makes them today. Hog hair had one big problem. It stayed wet, and wet bristles grow bacteria. In 1938, a company called DuPont made bristles out of nylon instead. Nylon dries. Nylon does not rot. Almost every brush has used it since.

notes: Plaque is a biofilm, not dirt

Fluoride helps enamel take minerals back

blocks.prompt: What the Brush Is Really For
blocks.text: Most people think brushing is about wiping off food. Mostly, it is not. The real target is plaque. Plaque is not dirt. It is alive. Within minutes of a cleaning, bacteria land on your enamel and glue themselves down. They build a sticky scaffold around themselves and invite other species in. Scientists call a structure like this a biofilm: a city of microbes living under a shared roof. Your mouth hosts hundreds of different species, and most of them are harmless or even useful. The trouble starts when you eat sugar. Certain bacteria, especially one called Streptococcus mutans, turn that sugar into acid. The acid sits against the tooth, trapped under the film, and pulls minerals out of the enamel. Do that often enough and the surface caves inward. That hole is a cavity. Here is the part that matters. Enamel is the hardest material your body makes, harder than bone, but it is not alive. Bone is threaded with cells that sense a break and rebuild it. Enamel is finished work. The cells that built it die once the tooth comes in, and nothing replaces them. A cavity waits for a dentist. Toothpaste helps, and fluoride helps a lot, because fluoride lets softened enamel take minerals back on and rebuilds the surface in a tougher form. But the main work is not chemical at all. It is mechanical. Bristles physically tear the biofilm apart before it can settle in and go to work. That is why two minutes beats two seconds, and why the back teeth, which almost everybody rushes, are where cavities usually show up first.

blocks.prompt: Two Minutes, Twice a Day, and Why Almost Nobody Does It
blocks.text: Ask a dentist how long you should brush and the answer has not changed in decades: two minutes, twice a day. Ask a researcher how long people actually brush and the answer comes back closer to forty five seconds. The gap between those two numbers explains a good deal of the dentistry done in the world. Brushing is a mechanical job. Plaque is a biofilm, a living layer of bacteria that anchors itself to enamel and thickens by the hour. No rinse dissolves a mature biofilm. It has to be broken apart by force. Bristles do that, and they need time and contact to do it, especially along the gumline and across the grooved chewing surfaces of the molars, where the film hides from a hurried brush. Technique matters more than effort. Scrubbing hard with stiff bristles does not clean better. It wears grooves into the enamel near the gum and pushes the gum tissue back, exposing the softer root underneath. That is why dentists almost always recommend soft bristles held at roughly forty five degrees toward the gumline, moved in small circles rather than sawed back and forth. The bristle tips themselves are rounded at the factory, tumbled against an abrasive until the cut ends are smooth, precisely so they sweep instead of scratch. Powered brushes are not a gimmick. Reviews pooling dozens of trials have found that oscillating and rotating heads remove measurably more plaque than a hand brush and reduce gum inflammation. Even so, a manual brush used well beats a powered brush used badly, and the built in timer may be doing as much good as the motor, because the timer is what solves the forty five second problem. None of this is expensive. A toothbrush costs less than a sandwich, needs no power, lasts three months, and holds off a disease that once cost ordinary people their teeth by middle age. In a 2003 survey, Americans were asked which invention they could least live without. The toothbrush finished first. It beat the car, the personal computer, and the cell phone.

6.title: The Brush That Fights an Invisible City

meta.templateLabel: The Brush That Fights an Invisible City

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Enamel is about 96 percent mineral
Enamel-building cells die when the tooth erupts
Streptococcus mutans ferments sugar into acid
Nylon bristles: DuPont, 1938
Army habit spread daily brushing in the US
About a billion US brushes discarded a year

blocks.prompt: The Cheapest Health Technology Ever Built
blocks.text: The toothbrush is not an impressive object. A stick of molded plastic, a few thousand nylon filaments, no moving parts, no power source, a price under two dollars. And yet in 2003, when a survey asked Americans which invention they could least live without, the toothbrush finished first, ahead of the automobile, the personal computer, and the cell phone. The vote reads like a joke until you understand what the brush is actually doing. It is not removing food. It is dismantling a city. Within minutes of a cleaning, bacteria settle onto the enamel and begin building. They secrete a sticky matrix, recruit other species into it, and organize into a biofilm: a layered, cooperative community with its own architecture and its own chemistry. Your mouth holds several hundred species, most of them harmless neighbors. But feed that community sugar and certain members, Streptococcus mutans chief among them, ferment it into acid. The acid is held against the tooth beneath the film, where saliva cannot wash it away, and it draws calcium and phosphate out of the enamel. Repeat the process often enough and the surface fails inward. That is a cavity, and it does not undo itself. The reason it does not undo itself is worth sitting with. Enamel is the hardest material the human body produces, harder than bone, roughly ninety six percent mineral by weight. It buys that hardness by giving something up. Bone is living tissue, threaded with cells that sense damage and rebuild. Enamel is finished work. The cells that laid it down die as the tooth erupts, and nothing replaces them. A broken arm knits. A broken tooth waits for a dentist. So the brush has one honest job: get the film off before the film gets to work. Toothpaste contributes, and fluoride contributes most, because fluoride lets softened enamel take minerals back on and rebuilds the surface in a form that resists acid better than the original did. But no paste and no rinse dissolves a mature biofilm. It has to be physically torn apart, which is why two minutes is not a suggestion, and why the back molars, with their deep grooves, collect most of the damage. Getting to this simple object took a long time. Babylonians frayed twigs into brushes more than five thousand years ago. Chinese makers set hog bristles into handles of bone and bamboo. In 1780 an Englishman named William Addis, jailed after a riot, drilled a saved dinner bone, threaded in bristles from a guard, and walked out with a business that still exists. Every one of those brushes carried the same flaw: animal hair holds water, and wet hair grows bacteria. The fix arrived in 1938, when DuPont replaced the hair with nylon. Nylon dried. Nylon did not rot. Brushing became something a person could safely do twice a day, and within a generation, helped along by army life drilling the habit into millions of returning soldiers, it became something Americans simply did without thinking. That solution came with a bill. Nylon and molded plastic do not decay either, which was rather the point of choosing them. By common estimate the United States discards around a billion toothbrushes a year, and almost none are recycled, because separating bonded filaments from a plastic handle costs more than the recovered material is worth. The property that made the toothbrush safe is the property that makes it permanent. Every brush you have ever used is still somewhere.
